title: Looping Over a Collection
intro: Rust has three ways to write `for x in …` over a list, and they differ in who owns the items afterwards. One borrows the list, one borrows it to change it, and one uses it up.

coming_from.go: `for n in &names` is `for _, n := range names`, and `v.iter().enumerate()` gives `i, n`. In Go `n` is a copy of the item, so you change items through the index. In Rust `for n in &mut nums` gives you a `&mut` reference to the item in the list (`*n *= 10` writes through it). `for n in names` (no `&`) has no Go counterpart: for a `Vec` it moves the items out, and `names` is gone.
coming_from.kotlin: `for n in &names` is `for (n in names)`, and `v.iter().enumerate()` is `withIndex()`. The loop variable in Kotlin is a `val` you cannot assign to; in Rust `for n in &mut nums` gives you a `&mut` reference to change the item through. Leave off the `&` and the loop takes ownership of a `Vec`, so you can't use it afterwards.
coming_from.python: `for n in &names` is Python's `for n in names`, and `v.iter().enumerate()` is `enumerate(names)`. In Python `n *= 10` only rebinds the name `n`; in Rust `for n in &mut nums` gives you a `&mut` reference to the item (`*n *= 10` writes through it). Leaving off the `&` moves the list into the loop, and `names` can no longer be used.
coming_from.typescript: `for n in &names` is `for (const n of names)`, and `v.iter().enumerate()` is `names.entries()`. In `for...of` a number `n` is a copy, so you assign through the index; in Rust `for n in &mut nums` gives you a `&mut` reference to the item (`*n *= 10` writes through it). Without the `&` the loop moves the list in, and it can't be used afterwards.
coming_from.java: `for n in &names` is your for-each: it reads each item and leaves the list alone. `for n in names` (no `&`) consumes the list, which a for-each never does. For numbers a Java loop variable is a copy, so you call `set(i, …)`; in Rust `for n in &mut nums` gives you a `&mut` reference to the item. Changing the objects in a list (`p.age++`) needs that `&mut` form too: `&names` is read-only.
coming_from.csharp: `for n in &names` is `foreach`, and `for n in &mut nums` changes items in place, where `foreach` does not let you assign to the loop variable. Writing `for n in names` without `&` uses a `Vec` up, so `names` is gone after the loop.
coming_from.c: Instead of an index loop, `for n in &nums` reads each item and `for n in &mut nums` hands you a `&mut` reference to change it in place. The length travels with the list, so there is no separate count to get wrong. Without the `&` the loop takes ownership of a `Vec`, and it can't be used afterwards.
coming_from.cpp: `for n in &v` is `for (const auto& n : v)`, and `for n in &mut v` is `for (auto& n : v)`. `for n in v` is the odd one: for a `Vec` it moves the items out and consumes `v`, rather than copying each one like `for (auto n : v)`.

notes: `for x in v` takes each item out of `v`; a `Vec` is used up (an array of numbers is copied, so it stays). `for x in &v` borrows each item; `v` stays. `for x in &mut v` borrows each item so you can change it.
`&v` is the same as `v.iter()`, and `&mut v` is the same as `v.iter_mut()`. With the borrowing forms `x` is a reference, so you may need `*x` to get the value.
Use the first form when you are done with the list and want to move its items somewhere else without copying them.
Do not add to or remove from a list inside a `for` over it: Rust refuses to compile it, and `retain` or a list of positions are the usual fixes.

gotcha.title: Looping, then using the list again
gotcha.looks_fine: In the other languages, a `for` loop over a list reads its items and the list is still there afterwards.
gotcha.rust_sees: `for n in names` (no `&`) hands the whole list to the loop. Each pass moves one `String` out into `n`, and the list's buffer is freed when the loop ends, so `names` cannot be used afterwards.
gotcha.why: This is the same move as in the Ownership lesson, hidden inside a loop. Rust makes you choose: add one `&` and the loop borrows, or leave it off to give the list away.

go.says: Go runs this and prints both names, then 2 names. `range` leaves the slice alone, so it is still there afterwards.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints both names, then 2 names. A `for` loop does not take the list away, so it is still there afterwards.

python.says: Python prints both names and then 2 names. A `for` loop does not take the list away, so it is still there afterwards.
python.code:
names = ["ana", "bo"]
for n in names:
    print(f"hi {n}")
print(f"{len(names)} names")

typescript.says: Prints both names, then 2 names. `for...of` does not take the array away, so it is still there afterwards.

java.says: A for-each loop in Java does not take the list away, so `names` is still there afterwards. Rust's `for n in names` uses the list up instead.

csharp.says: `foreach` does not take the list away, so `names` is still there afterwards and this prints 2 names.

c.says: A C index loop reads the array and nothing about it makes `names` unusable, so the length is still 2 afterwards.

cpp.says: `for (auto n : names)` copies each string, so `names` is untouched and still has 2 items. Rust's `for n in names` moves them out instead.

python.code:
names = ["ana", "bo"]

for n in names:
    print(f"hi {n}")

nums = [1, 2, 3]
for i in range(len(nums)):  # "n *= 10" would only rebind n, so assign through the index
    nums[i] *= 10

for i, n in enumerate(nums):
    print(f"{i}: {n}")
print(f"{len(names)} names, {nums}")

check-py.py.code:
# Backs the Python cells of the tables in lesson.mdx. Never shown.
v = ["ana", "bo", "cy"]
assert list(enumerate(v)) == [(0, "ana"), (1, "bo"), (2, "cy")]
assert list(zip(v, [31, 27])) == [("ana", 31), ("bo", 27)]
assert list(reversed(v)) == ["cy", "bo", "ana"]
assert v[::2] == ["ana", "cy"]
try:
    list(zip(v, [31, 27], strict=True))
    raise SystemExit("strict zip should raise")
except ValueError:
    pass
# removing the current item skips the next one, silently
v = [1, 2, 3, 4]
saw = []
for x in v:
    saw.append(x)
    if x == 2:
        v.remove(x)
assert v == [1, 3, 4] and saw == [1, 2, 4]
# appending: the loop reaches the new item
v = [1, 2, 3, 4]
saw = []
for x in v:
    saw.append(x)
    if x == 2:
        v.append(99)
assert saw == [1, 2, 3, 4, 99]
# a string loops over code points; a dict keeps insertion order
assert list("h\u00e9llo\U0001F600") == ["h", "\u00e9", "l", "l", "o", "\U0001F600"]
assert list({"b": 1, "a": 2, "c": 3}) == ["b", "a", "c"]
print("ok")
